title: Nanopulse stability log — sub-ms jitter scan
content:
Context / goal:
- Quick personal scratchpad for a focused scan: measure sub-millisecond jitter (p50/p95/p99/p999) under very light background load with short (<=32 token) responses. I call this the 'nanopulse' regime: small payloads, <1ms server compute on optimized kernels, where infra noise/gc/thread-wake dominates.

Why this matters:
- Product teams report intermittent UI hitches even at steady low QPS (2–6 qps per shard). Hypothesis: these are caused by rare wakeups, scheduler preemption, or minor contention in the request queue thread hop. If true, changes we make to hot-pool sizing, user-space spin waits, or prefetching could reduce p999 by 30–50%.

Test harness summary:
- Workload: synthetic HTTP/1 POST to hosted-edge instance (dev cluster) running model small-bert-quant (toy model used for quick loops). Response is unbatched, single-token generation trimmed to ~20 tokens to keep model compute minimal.
- Instrumentation: server-side high-resolution timestamps (nanosecond clock), Prom histograms (100us buckets down to 100ns), and client-side capture using wrk2 with high-resolution timers.
- Env: 4-core instance dev-edge-07, linux 6.x, golang runtime 1.21 for proxy. JVM noise avoided.
- Key parameters: concurrency=1, target-QPS=5 (steady), payload ~350 bytes. Run length 10 minutes per config.

Commands (notes to self, exact copies):
- prime run: ./scripts/invoke_burst.sh --qps 5 --dur 600 --concurrency 1 --url $DEV_EDGE
- detailed capture: sudo perf record -F 997 -g -- sleep 60 (during a 60s hotspot window)
- client: wrk -t1 -c1 -d10m -R5 --latency --script nanopulse.lua http://$DEV_EDGE/llm/generate

Observations (raw):
- Baseline (no extra tuning):
  - p50 ~ 0.78 ms
  - p95 ~ 1.9 ms
  - p99 ~ 3.6 ms
  - p999 ~ 12.4 ms (heavy tail observed ~1/1000)
  - sample histogram: tiny mode at 0.6–0.9 ms, long thin tail to 50ms, occasional spikes to 120ms (rare).
- With spin-wait tuned (spin=200us instead of 50us on request queue):
  - p50 ~ 0.80 ms (no meaningful change)
  - p95 ~ 1.6 ms (improvement ~15%)
  - p99 ~ 2.5 ms (improvement ~30%)
  - p999 ~ 4.6 ms (improvement ~63%)
  - Notes: p999 tightening suggests reduced cost of wakeups when worker threads are near-ready. CPU usage rose +3% but within headroom.
- With kernel tickless config + sched_latency_ns reduced (experimental system tweak):
  - Mixed results across runs; p95/p99 improved marginally but occasional worse-outliers at p999. Not stable across reboots.
- With light warm-cache priming (prefetch kv-cache for model keys before request):
  - p50 ~ 0.72 ms (small improvement)
  - p95 ~ 1.4 ms
  - p99 ~ 2.1 ms
  - p999 ~ 3.9 ms
  - Interpretation: priming reduces first-hop micro-IOs and marginally reduces jitter. Combined with spin-wait appears additive.

Telemetry snippets (client-side aggregated):
- 600s run, 3000 total requests per run (5 qps)
- tail sample counts: ~3 events >= 100ms across runs (very rare), most spikes fall in 3–10ms range.

What perf flame/stack traces showed (perf + go pprof):
- Spikes correlate with short periods where go runtime did a goroutine preemption combined with syscall for epoll wake. Stack top: runtime.netpoll, syscall.epoll_wait, internal queue handoff.
- A handful of events show unexpected futex contention inside the shared telemetry collector (lock acquisition cost ~50–200us).
- No evidence of DTLB or L3 thrash in perf samples for these runs.

Quick hypotheses (ranked):
1) Wakeup latency + short spin threshold: default spin too small -> sleeps and wakes cause large p999. Increasing spin reduces tail. (supported by measured improvement)
2) Lock contention on telemetry path contributes ~50–200us to some requests; in aggregate can push p999 upward. (evidence in perf)
3) Occasional OS-level preemption (background cron jobs, kernel threads) causes the very rare 100ms spikes; less actionable but can be mitigated by isolcpus for critical nodes.

Decisions / changes to try next (ordered, actionable):
- Short-term (low risk):
  1. Roll spin-wait change (spin 200us) to a small canary pool for serving runtime on 2 nodes in canary ring. Monitor p999 and CPU delta. (Jira INF-2142)
  2. Move telemetry aggregation to a per-thread ringbuffer and flush asynchronously to reduce futex collisions (PR draft: linked above). Bench locally then patch canary.
- Medium-term:
  3. Implement optional prefetch of model KV for short-gen paths (on warm pool entry) to avoid first-request micro-IOs.
  4. Add a lightweight watchdog that logs stack traces for requests > 10ms to gather more signal on tails.
- Longer-term:
  5. Experiment with isolcpus / realtime-affinity for hot serving nodes in dedicated capacity (requires infra approval).
  6. Consider an adaptive spin policy tuned by recent inter-arrival times (reduce CPU when idle, increase spin when frequent arrivals).

Open questions / risks:
- Spin increases CPU; we need to quantify cost at higher QPS (this run was 5 qps). Will spin help or hurt at 200 qps? (likely different dynamics — need separate experiment).
- Telemetry refactor could remove useful ordering guarantees — must ensure we preserve SLO-key metrics.
- Kernel tweaks are brittle across cloud images; prefer userland mitigations first.

Next experiments (short check-list):
- [ ] Canary spin change on 2 nodes for 24h, collect p999, cpu delta, and stack samples for spikes. (owner: Keira)
- [ ] Perf record of 10s windows around any p999 > 20ms event; attach to ticket. (owner: Omar)
- [ ] Implement per-thread ringbuffer telemetry prototype and microbench. (owner: Riley)
- [ ] Run a variant at QPS 50 and QPS 200 to see spin tradeoffs. (owner: Keira)

Notes to self / rough log of runs:
- 2025-11-03: baseline run (seed), observed 12.4ms p999.
- 2025-11-04: spin=200us trial — big tail improvement.
- 2025-11-06: priming experiment (kv prefetch) — additive effect.
- 2025-11-11: perf stacks show futex hits inside telemetry buffer lock.

Conclusion (working):
- For nanopulse regime at very low QPS, user-space spin tuning + small priming gives large wins on p999 with minimal CPU cost. Telemetry lock contention amplifies tails and is worth refactor. Kernel-level tweaks unstable and not recommended for general rollout.

Attached artifacts / where to look:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/734 (telemetry ringbuffer prototype)
- Jira: INF-2142 (canary spin rollout)
- Confluence notes: confluence:microburst-harmonies-2025 (working page with longer graphs)

Random thoughts:
- Might be worth adding a synthetic micro-API that returns near-zero but exercises the exact same code path as short-gen to separate model compute from runtime noise.
- Could also try per-request soft deadlines that trigger a cheap early path when a wakeup delay is suspected (risky for correctness).

-- Keira
(quick scratchpad; will clean up into a runbook if canary shows stable gains)
